newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Perry backs enlarged European security partnership.
newsitem.headline: Perry backs enlarged European security partnership.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry on Monday gave his backing to an enlarged military partnership taking in countries left out of the first wave of NATO's expansion into the formerly Communist east.

Perry said any countries unsuccessful in their bids to join the 16-member North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) as it grows could still play a role in Europe's new security model through an enlarged Partnership for Peace (PfP).

"My view is that they and NATO should work together in an expanded and strengthened Partnership for Peace...to help provide for the stability and security of all of Europe," Perry told a news conference during a four-nation visit to Europe.
The PfP, set up in 1993 to unite former European foes, has 27 member states, including Russia. It aims to boost military cooperation and political contact between NATO and non-members.
Since the end of the Cold War, a list of former Communist countries have been seeking to join NATO to guarantee security against any future threat from Russia.

The Baltic states of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which won independence from the former Soviet Union in 1991, are bidding for NATO membership as are Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Romania and Bulgaria.

NATO is not expected to make a firm decision on admitting new members until a summit in spring or summer 1997, but diplomatic sources say there is little hope for the bids made by the Baltic states, Romania or Bulgaria.
NATO is unwilling to provoke Russia by admitting the three Baltic states, which formed the western military flank of the former Soviet Union.

Russia's foreign minister Yevgeny Primakov on Friday repeated warnings to NATO that any extension of the military structure of the alliance towards its own western frontier would be "absolutely unacceptable".
Perry said that first and foremost any country had to satisfy a list of military and economic criteria to prove it was ready for NATO membership.
"NATO's position is that it is not seeking to enlarge or expand," Perry said before leaving Sweden for Denmark, where he will attend a closed-door Baltic Sea security seminar.
"NATO's view is that it is an institution that is open. It should not now or ever close itself to qualified members."

Perry said any country turned away by NATO should participate in the new European security model through PfP, which brings together non-aligned or neutral contries such as Sweden, Finland and Austria as well as ex-communist countries.
"I believe the Partnership for Peace provides for the security and stability of all of Europe," Perry said.
